evidence: "The hardware allows exactly three distinct offset modes, identified by the numeric codes 1, 2, and 3"; the survivor orders vertices by "descending degree for better pruning" and uses recursive constraint checking.
affordance_in_statement: The hardware allows exactly three distinct offset modes, identified by the numeric codes 1, 2, and 3. ... the sum of the squares of their assigned offset codes must be strictly greater than three times the square of the smaller of their two codes.
removal_suggestion: There is no semantics-preserving wording change that removes this: for codes 1, 2, and 3, the inequality is true exactly when the endpoint codes differ. To remove the shortcut, replace the scalar threshold with a genuinely nontrivial compatibility relation whose allowed pairs are not simply all unequal code pairs.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes the constraint as assigning one of three colors so adjacent vertices receive different colors, then applies degree-ordered backtracking.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: Exactly three numeric modes combined with the square-sum threshold.

common_affordance: The threshold permits exactly the pairs (1,2), (1,3), and (2,3), so every interaction merely requires different endpoint codes; the task is therefore general graph 3-colorability.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: It explicitly begins from "Try all 3^n assignments" and relies on insufficient backtracking/pruning, causing exponential-time execution at n=40.
It likewise uses naive assignment backtracking after noting that 3^40 is too large, but its pruning is not strong enough for worst-case graphs and it times out.

recommended_edit: Change the mutable threshold rule so that the allowed code pairs are a nontrivial, non-monochromatic compatibility relation rather than exactly the three unequal pairs; state it as an asymmetric or otherwise nonuniform phase-interaction rule in the scenario.
regression_risk: This changes the underlying constraint problem rather than merely its presentation; if the original inequality remains mathematically equivalent to unequal-color constraints, the surviving solver will still work.
